title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
authors: Sebastian Walch, Keith R. Fratus, Jan-Michael Reiner, Igor Lesanovsky
abstract: Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.
summary: This work analyzes the impact of shot noise on simulating quantum many-body systems using NMR spectra as a test case. By quantifying the required number of measurement shots, the authors show that the resource scaling is weak with system size. This suggests that statistical noise may not fundamentally limit the potential for quantum advantage in such simulations.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the statistical noise inherent in quantum measurements (shot noise) affects the ability to simulate complex quantum systems, specifically focusing on the scaling of required computational resources.
main_result: The required number of measurement shots needed to achieve a desired accuracy scales only weakly with the system size, suggesting that shot noise does not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in NMR simulation.
method: The authors analyze the scaling of the infidelity between the noisy quantum simulation result and the exact reference result by expanding the cosine similarity in powers of the noise.
model_or_system: The test case is the simulation of Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra, modeled by coupled nuclear spin systems governed by Heisenberg or Ising Hamiltonians. The simulation is mapped onto a qubit register for quantum computation.
key_observables: The required number of shots ($R$), the spectral noise covariance ($	ext{Cov}[\epsilon_R]$), and the resulting infidelity ($1 - C(s_R, s)$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$, number of nuclei), desired accuracy, and the number of shots ($R$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses solely on shot noise, neglecting other error sources like decoherence or Trotterization errors, and relies on expanding the fidelity metric to second order in the noise.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares NMR spectroscopy across physical, classical (exponential), and quantum (shot-noise limited) regimes. Other figures detail numerical results for both Ising and Heisenberg model Hamiltonians across varying system sizes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by comparing classical and quantum simulation scaling, then develops the theoretical framework by calculating the single-shot variance and deriving the scaling of the infidelity with $R$ using the Central Limit Theorem.
why_interesting: It directly addresses a critical practical hurdle for quantum computation—measurement noise—by providing quantitative bounds on resource scaling for a physically relevant many-body problem like NMR.
